newsitem.title: USA: Pacificorp, Energy Group deal coming soon - source.
newsitem.headline: Pacificorp, Energy Group deal coming soon - source.

text.p: Pacificorp has agreed to buy Britain's Energy Group Plc for $6 billion in cash and plans to sell its Pacific Telecom unit to help finance the deal, a source close to Pacificorp said.

"The transaction is clearly going forward and an announcement will be made as soon as this week or early next week," said the source on Thursday. "The financing package is being feverishly worked on and is what is causing a delay," he said.
Terms of the deal would call for Pacificorp to pay about $6 billion in cash and assume another $4 billion in debt.

The source said financing could come from the spinoff of Pacific Telecom, which provides local telephone service to rural and suburban customers in the west, Midwest and Alaska. Discussions regarding the sale of the division, which could fetch $1.5 billion, are under way, the source said.

"There would be no shortage of interested parties for Pacific Telecom," said Lloyd Greif, president of Greif and Co., a Los Angeles investment bank, noting that a list of likely bidders would include GTE Corp., SBC Communications Inc., and MCI Communications Corp.
Energy Group, formed earlier this year through a spin-off of energy assets by Hanson Plc, said this week it was holding talks with Pacificorp and was expecting an offer soon.
Energy Group, Britain's biggest electricity distributor, said any offer would be expected to be priced at a premium of around 20 percent to its share price.
Portland, Ore.-based Pacificorp has declined to comment on the acquisition, which would nearly double its size, expand its geographic reach and make it a global energy provider.
The source said the deal was initiated by Pacificorp. "They approached Energy and they did so because they identified it as a perfect fit," said the source.
Nevertheless, industry experts said the deal could raise concerns with state utility regulators and consumer groups.

"The risk lies in if one of the seven states decides to raise a stink about what is going to happen to the quality of (PacifiCorp's) balance sheet," said Dan Ford, an analyst at HSBC James Capel. "Unless there is some sort of financial magic, their debt rating will drop," he noted.

PacifiCorp provides retail electric service to customers in California, Idaho, Montana, Oregon, Utah, Washington and Wyoming. It also owns a regional electricity distributor in Australia and a Texas-based natural gas company.
Although state utility commissions do not have strict jurisdiction over an acquisition by PacifiCorp, they do have jurisdiction over the sale of the telecommunications business.
In addition, the commissions are likely to watch out for any impact on electricity customers in their states.

"We would be involved if they want to issue securities through the Pacific Power and Light operation," said Phil Nyegaard, administrator of the financial analysis division of the Oregon Public Utility Commission.
Ford noted the state commissions "have very broad powers to make comments and suggest outcomes."

Consumer groups are also monitoring the deal. Bob Jenks, executive director of Citizens' Utility Board of Oregon, said the group was concerned a new international focus would shift PacifiCorp's attention from its retail electricity business.
"What's going to happen to the customer here?" he asked, citing complaints against PacifiCorp following its closing of regional offices and centralized customer service operations.
But most analysts said the deal was unlikely to present antitrust concerns, with little overlap seen between operations of the two companies.

Sources continued to stress the likely synergies between PacifiCorp's coal mining and generating assets and Energy Group's Peabody coal unit as well as the good geographical fit of the company's power marketing arms.
"I don't see any regulatory impediments," said Ed Tirello at NatWest Securties. "Portland would become the headquarters for one of the biggest utilities in the world."
